    If Sergeant Stubby proved what an untrained stray could do in the First World War, Chips proved what a dog could do once the United States built an actual program around him. Chips became the most decorated American dog of World War II. His story also marks the moment the Army decided it should never again give such awards to an animal.

    In a recent development, chips was a mix of German Shepherd, Collie, and Husky, born around 1940 and raised as a family pet by Edward Wren and his family in Pleasantville, Newly introduced York. In 1942, the Wrens donated Chips to the newly formed Dogs for Defense program, part of the Armyâs larger War Dog Program, formally authorized on March 13, 1942. Chips trained at the War Dog Training Center in Front Royal, Virginia, and was partnered with Private John P. Rowell. The two served in the 3rd Military Police Platoon, 30th Infantry Regiment, 3rd Infantry Division, under General George S. Patton.

    Chips and Rowell landed in North Africa during Operation Torch in November 1942 and served through campaigns in Sicily, Italy, southern France, and the Rhineland and central European theaters. He was also present as a sentry dog at the 1943 Casablanca Conference, guarding the meeting between Winteon Churchill and Franklin D. Roosevelt.

    Chips earned his fame during the Allied invasion of Sicily, Operation Husky, on the morning of July 10, 1943. As Rowell and Chips came ashore, a hidden machine gun nest opened fire and pinned down their platoon. Chips tore free of his handler and charged the position alone, seizing the gunner by the throat and forcing the crew to surrender. As a result, four Italian soldiers surrendered. That same night, Chips alerted the platoon to ten additional enemy soldiers attempting to slip through the lines under cover of darkness, leading to their capture as well.

    Chips did not escape the encounter unscathed. He suffered burns around his mouth and eye and a wound to his scalp. His actions, however, swiftly became national news. Captain Edward G. Parr, the tech giant commander, recommended Chips for the Distinguished Service Cross, citing his âcourageous action in single-handedly eliminating a dangerous machine gun nest and causing surrender of its crewâ. On November 19, 1943, Major General Lucian K. Truscott Jr. awarded Chips the Silver Star, and accounts differ slightly on whether the Distinguished Service Cross was also formally conferred or only recommended. What is well documented is that Chips also received a Purple Heart for his wounds.

    In 1945, Chips met General Dwight (Ike) D. Eisenhower, who bent down to pet the famous dog. Chips, true to his sentry training, nipped the generalâs hand. The incident became one of the more good-humored footnotes in his legend.

    Washington reacted less good-humoredly to the idea of a dog receiving human military honors. After public objection to the precedent of awarding animals medals intended for soldiers, the War Department revoked Chipsâs Silver Star, Distinguished Service Cross, and Purple Heart in early 1944. His platoon nonetheless unofficially awarded him a Theater Ribbon with Arrowhead, an honor reserved for assault landings, along with eight battle stars, one for each campaign in which he served. Chips was honorably discharged on December 10, 1945, and returned to the Wren family in Pleasantville. He died a few months after returning home, from complications related to his wartime wounds.

    Sources indicate that in January 2018, more than seven decades after his service, the United Kingdomâs PDSA posthumously awarded Chips its Dickin Medal, the animal equivalent of the Victoria Cross, in a ceremony at the Churchill War Rooms in London on the 75th anniversary of the Casablanca Conference. John Wren, then 76, traveled from the United States to accept the medal on Chipsâs behalf. PDSA Director General Jan McLoughlin remarked that the honor finally allowed Chips to âtake his place in the history books as one of the most heroic dogs to serve with the US Armyâ.

    Chips is estimated to have been one of more than 10,000 dogs who served in the American military during World War II. His story, and the controversy his medals caused, shaped military policy for decades: no American war dog would again receive an official human combat decoration, a policy that held until working dogs began receiving other forms of formal recognition much later in the twentieth century.

    Every military working dog story, whether it unfolded in the trenches of World War I or on a patrol in Afghanistan, is also the story of a partnership. Learning that history is one of the simplest ways to honor the generations of dogs and handlers who served side by side. If these stories have moved you, there are meaningful ways to help carry them forward.

    Support retired dogs. Not every military working dog can retire to a family couch. The Ddamien Project provides lifelong homes for retired military, contract, and law enforcement dogs whose medical or behavioral needs make typical adoption difficult.

    Learn more. The Military Working Dog Heritage Museum, founded by former K9 handlers, is gathering the photographs, documents, and firsthand accounts of the dogs and people who served. Its newsletter, The Paw Print, shares many of these stories with the public.

    It has been revealed that keep today's working dogs strong. Canine Advancement Group, led by veterinarian Dr. Brian Farr, advocates for treating working dogs as the athletes they are, offering evidence-based guidance on fitness, welfare, and handler education.

    Follow the national tribute. The National Service Animals Monument, planned for Washington, DC, will honor service animals and their handlers across military, law enforcement, and assistance roles, including generations of military working dogs.

    Sources indicate that these dogs are part of our history. By preserving their stories, honoring their service, and caring for the dogs still serving and those who have come home, we help make sure their legacy endures.

    Among the dogs of the 26th Infantry Scout Dog Platoon, one German Shepherd stood out for the length and success of its combat record. Scout Dog York is credited with taking part in 148 combat missions without a single man in his patrol being killed, a record that made him one of the war's most celebrated scout dogs.

She serves as the Social Media Coordinator for both the Military Working Dog Heritage Museum and the National Service Animals Monument.     How to Winterize an Outdoor Faucet – This 5-Minute Job Could Save You Thousands

    📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1182 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, picture a hose still screwed onto the spigot in December.
    • It's a fall chore, best done the same day you winterize sprinklers.
    • It has been revealed that outdoor faucet winterization is mostly about getting water out and keeping it from getting trapped again.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, picture a hose still screwed onto the spigot in December. The water behind it has nowhere to go. Once nights stay below 32°F (0°C), it can freeze solid, and copper and brass don't have much give. Something splits. That repair bill usually runs well past what the faucet cost, so it pays to sort out how to winterize an outdoor faucet now.

    It's a fall chore, best done the same day you winterize sprinklers. The annoying part is where the damage hides. From the yard, the faucet can look fine while the pipe behind it has cracked a few inches inside the wall. Nobody sees that until the water's back on.

    It has been revealed that outdoor faucet winterization is mostly about getting water out and keeping it from getting trapped again. Take off the hose, shut off the supply, drain what's left, and add a cover for backup. Try to finish alongside your other gardening winterizing tasks, and before the first hard freeze indicates up in the forecast.

    Industry observers note that if you only get to one step today, make it this one. Any hose left on the spigot holds water inside the faucet, and that goes for frost-free models too – the water has nowhere to drain while the hose is attached. Splitters, watering timers, and quick-connect fittings trap water the same way, so pull them all off.

    Then empty the hose. Stretch it down a slope or drape loops over a fence rail so the water runs out both ends. Leftover water can freeze and split it, and a drained hose stored out of the weather generally holds up longer. Suncast's 100-foot Hose Hideaway from Walmart keeps a coiled hose off the ground under a lid.

    It has been revealed that start inside. Standard faucets usually have their own shutoff, somewhere close to where the pipe goes out through the wall, often in a basement, crawl space, or utility room. Look up between the ceiling joists, too. A round handle turns clockwise until it stops. If it's a lever, a quarter turn puts it crosswise to the pipe, and that's closed.

    Not every home has one, and older houses often don't, which makes it harder to winterize hose bib lines without shutting off water to the whole house. If you're not sure what an unlabeled valve is, leave it alone. Close the wrong one, and it's no fun to find out halfway through washing dishes. Frost-free faucets, like this SharkBite one, work differently and may not need this step.

    Industry observers note that for faucets without a dedicated indoor shutoff, a Freeze Miser outdoor faucet protector offers another option. It screws onto the spigot and automatically releases a small amount of water when the water temperature drops below 37°F (3°C), helping prevent freezing. Unlike conventional winterizing, this method requires leaving the water supply on and the outdoor faucet fully open.

    It has been revealed that head back outside and open the faucet all the way. Some water should run out, slow to a trickle, and stop. Did it keep flowing? Then the indoor valve isn't closed all the way, or it's not the right valve at all.

    According to recent reports, some shutoffs have a little cap on the side, called a bleeder. Leave the outdoor faucet open so air can get in, set a bucket underneath, and back the cap off slowly. Water will dribble out. When it quits, screw the cap back on. Many plumbers will leave the outdoor faucet open all winter. Some valve makers say to close it, though, so go by whatever came with yours.

    An outdoor faucet cover holds in a little of the warmth that seeps through the wall from inside. The rigid type (like the image above) is a foam-lined dome with a cord that pulls it snug against the siding. Home Depot's Everbilt hard outdoor faucet cover is a good cheap option. Flexible pouches go on more like a sock (see image below), and the Thinsulate-lined faucet socks on Amazon come two to a pack.

    Recent findings suggest that either kind should sit flat against the wall with no gap for cold air. Check it after windy nights, because covers do get knocked loose. It's backup, not a substitute for unhooking hoses and draining the line, and outdoor spigot winter protection still starts with an empty faucet. An Ambient Weather Wi-Fi weather station can send temperature alerts to your phone before a hard freeze.

    In a recent development, plenty of people hear frost-free and figure that means forget about it. That's about half right, maybe. From the yard, a frost-free outdoor faucet looks like any other spigot. Its handle turns a long stem, and the part that stops the water sits way back at the end of it, where it's warmer. Close it, and the water in that stem should run out the spout. That only works if the faucet slopes a little toward the outside.

    So the hose still comes off, or water stays put and can freeze inside the wall, often unnoticed until spring. Damage, a level installation, or a pipe running through an unheated crawl space can leave one vulnerable too.

    Sources indicate that correctly installed ones usually don't need the supply shut off and drained, but the manufacturer's instructions get the final say. Homes without an indoor shutoff can have a plumber fit a replacement such as the SharkBite one mentioned above.

    It has been revealed that if the faucet won't run or ice has formed around the spout, skip the torch, even if one happens to be sitting right there in the garage. No open flame, and nothing else that blasts heat at it, either. There's framing and insulation right behind that siding. Hair dryers are slower. Point it at the faucet and the wall around it and give it time. Keep the cord out of puddles.

    Suspect a leak? Shut off the water to that line, or the main valve if there's no separate one, and call a plumber. Frozen pipe damage isn't always visible right away. A crack of ⅛ inch (3 mm) can let out up to 250 gallons (946L) a day, and it may not drip at all until the ice thaws or the water goes back on.

    Most of what it takes to protect outdoor faucets from freezing – and to prevent frozen pipes behind them – is getting the water out and keeping it out. Get that done before the first hard frost, and the faucet should be ready come spring, with dry walls behind it.

    Forget Poinsettias! This Colorful Christmas Houseplant Is Easier To Grow And Blooms For Ages

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Poinsettias might be the traditional choice for festive decorating, but they're not the only Christmas houseplants capable of bringing a splash of holiday color indoors.

    If you're looking for something a little different this year, there is a holiday plant that promises the same bold red hues of a poinsettia, along with glossy succulent leaves and a surprisingly easygoing nature. And no, we're not talking about sweet box (although that's also a brilliant container plant to add to your shopping list).

    Instead, we're dragging the beautiful Flaming Katy (Kalanchoe blossfeldiana) into the spotlight, as its flowers can last for weeks, making it a lovely way to brighten your home through the darker months.

    Blooming in the fall and winter, what could be prettier than this Flaming Katy at Christmas?

    It has been revealed that often sold as a seasonal flowering plant, Flaming Katy is actually a tender perennial succulent, which means you don't necessarily have to throw it away once Christmas is over. In fact, all you have to do is give it the right conditions and it can continue growing for years, potentially rewarding you with another spectacular display.

    Recent findings suggest that there's no denying that poinsettias look impressive, but they can be surprisingly fussy about their surroundings, as they dislike cold draughts and sudden temperature changes – so much so that their leaves can drop. Overwatering is another common problem, particularly when plants are left sitting in decorative pots without adequate drainage.

    Sources indicate that flaming Katy offers a much easier alternative, as its leaves store water, helping it cope with occasional dry spells, while its clusters of brightly colored flowers provide plenty of festive impact. Red is a particularly popular choice for Christmas, of course, although you can also find varieties with pink, orange, yellow and white flowers, too.

    Better still? Rather than providing a brief burst of colour, a healthy plant can remain in bloom for several weeks, sometimes even longer depending on the variety and growing conditions.

    Unlike some Christmas houseplants, this one doesn't need constant attention to keep looking good. Once you find a suitable position (a birght windowsill is ideal), the main thing is to avoid overwatering and make sure it receives enough light.

    Sources indicate that it also prefers average indoor humidity, so there's no need to mist it or create a particularly humid environment; in fact, good air circulation is more useful than excessive moisture around the leaves. Just keep it somewhere warm, ideally with temperatures around 60–75°F (16–24°C), and give it plenty of bright, indirect light (and remember that some gentle morning sunshine is generally welcome, too).

    During the flowering period, you can remove individual faded flower clusters to keep the plant looking tidy, but there's no need for complicated pruning or constant feeding.

    Industry observers note that perhaps the best thing about Flaming Katy is that, even though it's a Christmas houseplant, it doesn't have to be a disposable festive decoration; once flowering finishes, you can continue growing it as a foliage houseplant. With the right care, it can produce latest growth and flower again.

    Industry observers note that oh sure, poinsettias will always have their place in Christmas decorating, but Flaming Katy makes a convincing alternative if you'd prefer something colorful, undemanding and potentially longer-lasting when it comes to brightening up a home during winter. And unlike a certain fussy red plant that pops up everywhere in the holidays, this little flowering succulent really can stick around for years.

    Hey, a festive purchase that really does keep on giving? Consider us sold!

    What Your Jade Plant Needs in November – 5 Easy Ways to Unlock Lush Growth and Good Fortune in the Latest Year

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1672 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • With its sculptural trunk, plump leaves, and reputation as a symbol of prosperity and good fortune, a healthy jade plant (Crassula ovata) can thrive for decades.
    • In a recent development, shorter days mean weaker sunlight streaming through the glass, while central heating inevitably clicks on.
    • Luckily, protecting your jade now is oh-so-simple.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    With its sculptural trunk, plump leaves, and reputation as a symbol of prosperity and good fortune, a healthy jade plant (Crassula ovata) can thrive for decades. Yet as November settles in, these plants quietly shift into semi-dormancy as less sun naturally fills the space. This can make a jade feel vulnerable if your care routine stays stuck in summer mode.

    In a recent development, shorter days mean weaker sunlight streaming through the glass, while central heating inevitably clicks on. Stand beside a sunny windowsill in the afternoon and it can feel cozy, yet by evening an icy chill radiates off the pane. Because of this, your jade plant care routine needs to adapt. It would be foolish to water as you did months earlier, or leave a prized specimen pressed against a drafty sill. If you’re not careful, you might risk triggering leaf drop, soft stems, or weak and leggy growth.

    Luckily, protecting your jade now is oh-so-simple. Just a few seasonal adjustments prevent calamity, so you can preserve those glossy, coin-shaped leaves, and even encourage delicate star-shaped winter blooms. And for anyone looking to boost their fortunes in the upcoming year, it all starts here and now by giving your beloved jade plants the right care and attention. Here’s how to help yours thrive through winter, so it sees in spring in the very best shape.

    Industry observers note that jade plant care this month comes down to balancing your own comfort against your plant’s natural seasonal rhythm. While you turn up the thermostat and pull the curtains against the dark, your jade craves bright, crisp days, cool nights, and dry feet. Even innocently shifting a pot aside to make room for holiday decor can plunge your sun-loving succulent into stressful gloom or into the path of a radiator blast.

    Your local climate and USDA hardiness zone still shape indoor care. In northern regions (zones 3-6), dry furnace air and frosty windowpanes pose the biggest threats. In mild coastal or southern regions (zones 9-11), anyone who risks keeping jades outdoors on patios must watch for cool rainstorms that might waterlog pots.

    Sources indicate that before starting your tasks, clear any dust off the leaves with a soft brush so they absorb maximum winter light. If you fancy a closer look at your jade plant’s nooks and crannies, invest in a magnifying glass or a loupe, like the JarLink 30X 60X Illuminated Jeweler’s Loupe, available on Amazon. This can help you spot early mealybug fluff or scale bumps. It’s also a good idea to verify that drainage holes aren't blocked, before you start these essential jade care tasks.

    Scaling back your watering routine is the single most impactful step you can take for a jade plant in November. As daylight dwindles and growth slows to a crawl, jade roots absorb moisture more slowly than they did in summer. Leaving roots sitting in a damp potting mix for weeks at a time invites fungal root rot. Before reaching for the watering can, push your index finger 1-2 inches (2.5-5cm) down into the soil, insert a plain wooden chopstick to the bottom. Alternatively, use a probe like the inexpensive XLUX Plant Soil Moisture Meter from Amazon.

    Sources indicate that if any dampness or dark soil clings to it, wait another week. When the mix is dry, water thoroughly until excess drains out the bottom hole. Empty the saucer immediately. Keep plant age and variety in mind. Compact varieties like Hobbit and Gollum, or young plants in small 4-inch (10cm) pots, dry out faster than massive specimens in deep tubs. Avoid over-correcting: if lower leaves feel thin, soft, or wrinkled, your jade plant is ready for a drink.

    In a recent development, by November, the sun sits lower in the sky and a jade that did fine in an east or west window all summer may only catch a sliver of the light it needs now. Jade plants require at least 4-6 hours of bright, direct light daily to keep stems sturdy and leaves compact. This is especially true of variegated cultivars like Tricolor or Variegata, which have less chlorophyll and lose their creamy-pink margins in dim rooms. Relocate your jade to an unobstructed south-facing window or a bright west-facing sill. Make the move gradually over 3-4 days so leaves do not scorch.

    Sources indicate that watch for early signs of light starvation, such as pale new leaves or elongated stems with wide gaps between leaf pairs (known as etiolation). If natural winter light falls short in northern latitudes, supplement with a full-spectrum LED grow bulb positioned 12-18 inches (30-45cm) above the canopy for 10-12 hours daily. Feit Electric's 9-Watt BR30 Medium E26 Full-Spectrum LED Grow Light Bulb from The Home Depot will screw into a plain old lamp socket. Switch your grow lights off at night, though. Uninterrupted dark, cool nights trigger mature jades to set flower buds.

    Recent findings suggest that put your palm on the window glass one of these chilly mornings, and you'll know why the sill can be a rough spot. Jade has zero tolerance for frost or abrupt temperature shifts. Leaves pressed against a freezing pane can get damaged even indoors. Pull your potted jade back 3-6 inches (8-15cm) from cold windowpanes, and slide a piece of insulating cork or folded cloth beneath the pot on chilly stone or marble sills.

    Recent findings suggest that also keep jades clear of exterior entry doors that blast icy air every time someone walks in, as well as radiators and heaters: neither extreme is a good neighbor for a jade, really. Aim for steady daytime temperatures between 60-75°F (16-24°C) and nights around 50-55°F (10-13°C), which keeps growth compact and encourages winter flower buds. You can pick up a digital thermometer to take the guesswork out of it, such as the ThermoPro TP50 Digital Indoor Thermometer, available from Walmart, which can also flag up drafts you might not otherwise notice.

    It has been revealed that in November, the best thing you can do with your bottle of houseplant fertilizer is tuck it away in a cupboard until spring. Jade plants grow very little in the dark months: feeding them won't change that. They enter a natural dormancy phase during short, low-light winter days, and their roots can’t process the extra nutrients. Feeding a dormant succulent just forces out weak, pale shoots that stretch awkwardly toward the window and snap easily under their own weight.

    According to recent reports, unused fertilizer salts can also accumulate rapidly in dry winter potting mix, burning delicate roots and leaving crusty mineral deposits. Whether you tend a classic green jade plant or a trailing Ripple Jade, hold off on all feeding until February. If you did feed in October, that's fine – just don't follow it up! Once bright spring sunlight sparks fresh leaf tips, you can resume feeding every 6-8 weeks through summer. At that point, use a balanced liquid succulent or houseplant fertilizer diluted to half strength.

    Industry observers note that warm, dry indoor heating creates prime breeding conditions for sap-sucking houseplant pests, making a thorough inspection essential. Tip your pot gently toward bright window light and check the undersides of leaves and stem junctions. Look for tufts of white fuzz or sticky leaves: these are the telltale signs of citrus mealybugs (Planococcus citri). Any flat, brown, shell-like bumps are scale (Coccus hesperidum).

    It has been revealed that quarantine affected plants. Dip a cotton swab in 70% isopropyl rubbing alcohol, such as Equate 70% Isopropyl Rubbing Alcohol from Walmart. Dab pests to dissolve their waxy protective coatings, repeating weekly until gone. Keep your jade plant in quarantine for a few weeks. Avoid insecticidal soaps on jade plants. Clemson University’s Home & Garden Information Center warns that fatty-acid soaps can damage jade foliage. While inspecting, pinch off any yellowing lower leaves. Dropping a few older bottom leaves after a fall move is normal. However, dark, mushy stems signal rot, requiring immediate action.

    When a jade plant looks tired in November, resist the urge to try to fix everything at once. You might want to pull it out, give it a new pot and take the pruners to it, but you need to hold off on this. Roots that get disturbed now don't grow back quickly, and big pruning cuts made now won't see new growth for months. Save routine repotting and shaping shears for spring, using a fast-draining cactus mix such as Espoma CA4 Organic Cactus Mix, available from Walmart, when the time comes.

    The only reason to repot now is if your plant has a rot emergency. If stems feel soft or the pot emits a sour odor, slide the plant out of its pot immediately. Trim away brown, rotted roots and soft stem tissue with sterilized snips. Let the calluses dry for a couple of days, then pot your jade into fresh, dry cactus mix. Hold off on water for a full week afterward. Don't let worry turn into extra watering. Too much water is one of the quickest ways to lose a jade in winter.

    Caring for a jade plant in November is less about doing more, and more about stepping back thoughtfully. By scaling back your watering can, moving plants into bright southern light, guarding against chilly windows and drafts, shelving fertilizer, and keeping an eye out for winter pests, your jade will thrive. With a little attention now (and some cool, dark nights on your side), your jade may even reward you with pretty star-shaped winter blooms, before pushing out new leaves in spring.

His growing success indicates that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

    #21463. What Your Coneflowers Need in November – 5 Tips to Get Them Winter-Ready and Help Backyard Birds

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (952 w)

    What Your Coneflowers Need in November – 5 Tips to Get Them Winter-Ready and Help Backyard Birds

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (952 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Coneflowers (Echinacea spp.) are tough, low-maintenance perennials that are staples in many gardens.
    • In a recent development, though considered low-care perennials, these flowers are about as close to no-care as a flower can be.
    • I’ve pulled together a list of the top five things to do – or not do – to your coneflowers in November while you're busy winterizing the garden.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Coneflowers (Echinacea spp.) are tough, low-maintenance perennials that are staples in many gardens. Their tall blooms bring long-lasting color and attract pollinators like bees and butterflies.

    In a recent development, though considered low-care perennials, these flowers are about as close to no-care as a flower can be. By the time November rolls around, these beautiful plants don’t need much. In fact, when you are growing coneflowers, it’s more important to know what to avoid than to complete a task list.

    I’ve pulled together a list of the top five things to do – or not do – to your coneflowers in November while you're busy winterizing the garden. The primary goals are wildlife support, disease control, and frost protection.

    Industry observers note that coneflowers bloom with cheerful, daisy-like flowers from early summer through fall. By November, the plants have faded, and cutting them back may seem like the obvious next step.

    But don’t be tempted to prune coneflowers in the fall unless you are a total garden neatnik. It’s far better to wait to prune until spring. If you leave the dried seed heads standing, you give songbirds a valuable food source to help them make it through the winter. Goldfinches, chickadees, and cardinals will thank you. In addition, the hollow stems of the coneflowers provide habitat for overwintering beneficial insects. Proposal to prune them in early spring.

    In a recent development, every rule has an exception, and it’s best not to prune coneflowers in November unless the foliage is diseased. Whenever you see sick foliage – in this case, coneflowers with powdery mildew, leaf spots, or aster yellows – it’s high time for a haircut.

    Cut back any diseased or pest-infested coneflower stalks to a few inches above the soil. Toss all the trimmings in the trash, not the compost heap. Don’t forget to sanitize your pruners between plants and after you are done. Equate 91% Isopropyl Alcohol from Walmart is a handy option – simply dilute it to around 70% before using it to disinfect the blades.

    According to recent reports, if powdery mildew is a recurring problem, consider keeping Bonide Neem Oil Spray on hand for next growing season. Applied at the first signs of infection, it can help control the disease and prevent it from spreading, provided the product label covers the intended use.

    Recent findings suggest that coneflowers are hardly prima donnas, but they do insist on well-draining soil. Waterlogged soil causes root and crown rot in coneflowers, sad endings for such beautiful perennials.

    It has been revealed that the easiest way to check your flowers’ drainage is to wait for a late autumn rain. Let the rain do its thing, then – after an hour or two – head out to the coneflower bed and take a look. If you see standing water or water pooling on the soil for hours after the rain stops, your drainage is poor.

    Poor drainage is not a death sentence. You can remedy this by layering a mixture of compost and, where appropriate, horticultural grit, such as this 1–2 mm coarse horticultural grit from Home Depot. This will redirect the flow of water away from the core roots.

    You can consider transplanting the perennial in spring to a location with better drainage.

    According to recent reports, organic mulch helps keep your coneflowers’ roots protected through the winter. Spread a loose layer – 2 to 3 inches (5–7.5 cm) deep – around the base of the plants to shield the root zone from extreme temperatures and keep weeds away.

    In a recent development, A natural shredded mulch, such as Miracle-Gro Organic All Natural Mulch from Home Depot, is a good choice. But take care: don’t let the mulch touch the main crown, or crown rot may develop.

    Industry observers note that perennials with their roots in the ground are less vulnerable to winter temperatures than potted plants. While coneflowers are tall plants with stems that can reach 4 feet (1.2 m), dwarf varieties grow well in containers.

    These smaller perennials will come back every year if you provide them adequate winter protection. First, move the containers close to a structure in a sheltered spot. The Bamworld rolling plant caddies from Amazon make moving heavy pots much easier.

    If your hardiness zone is USDA 5–9, you may be able to overwinter them outside with adequate protection. Mound mulch around the pots for insulation, or try the leaf insulation trick. For extra protection, wrap the containers in a layer of Valibe frost-protection fabric.

    In cooler zones, move your potted coneflowers into a cold, unheated garage or shed where their roots will be protected from extreme freezing temperatures. Keep the soil barely moist through dormancy, but never waterlogged, and empty any saucers after watering.

    Think of these four tasks as the biggest things NOT to do with coneflowers in November. Avoiding them will almost guarantee your coneflowers greet spring happy and healthy.

    #21459. Lavender Plant Care Made Easy: Your Complete Planting Guide for Lush and Lovely Blooms Year After Year

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 16m • 📚 Deep Dive (3153 w)

    Lavender Plant Care Made Easy: Your Complete Planting Guide for Lush and Lovely Blooms Year After Year

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3153 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

    ⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Legend has it that one of my earliest gardening forays involved a large lavender bush.
    • Few garden pleasures rival the velvety fix of fingers dancing along a billowing carpet of lavender wands on a languid summer afternoon.
    • It has been revealed that bizarrely, lavender has a bit of a reputation for being tricky to grow, but the truth is that it’s the ultimate garden rebel.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Legend has it that one of my earliest gardening forays involved a large lavender bush. As a toddler, I fell sideways into a mound of perfumed purple blooms and just lay there on my back, gazing at the bobbling petals, apparently with a look of absolute joy on my face. As a grown-up, the joy of lavender is still very much a thing. I may try to be more careful about where I stand these days, but my fascination with this sun-kissed fragrant icon is only getting more pronounced with time.

    Few garden pleasures rival the velvety fix of fingers dancing along a billowing carpet of lavender wands on a languid summer afternoon. Beyond its timeless fragrance, lavender offers constant, lyrical movement and enduring cottage garden prettiness that seems to work in a range of palettes and plant combinations. Throw in a chorus of bumblebees drunk on nectar and swinging on those violet spires, and you can see why it’s so easy to fall head over heels for this Mediterranean beauty.

    It has been revealed that bizarrely, lavender has a bit of a reputation for being tricky to grow, but the truth is that it’s the ultimate garden rebel. While many perennials long for luxuriant loam and scoops of compost, lavender is sculpted by lean, rocky soils and blistering sun, and it isn’t that hard to harness its intoxicating essential oils and maintain a tight, sturdy habit. Whether you want a petite purple knot garden or a sun-drenched lavender planter, this enduring favorite deserves a spot in every yard. Here’s how to ensure your plants return year after year with lush, aromatic blooms.

    Recent findings suggest that lavandula spp. (L. angustifolia, L. stoechas, L. dentata, L. × intermedia).

    Woody sub-shrub / evergreen perennial.

    1-3 feet (30-90cm) depending on species.

    Well-drained, sandy, gravelly, or gritty loam (pH 6.5-7.5, alkaline-leaning).

    It has been revealed that USDA zones 5-10 (Not in the US? Convert your zone).

    Spring-Summer (May-September, varies by species).

    Mediterranean basin, southern Europe, northern Africa, southwest Asia, and the Arabian Peninsula.

    Before picking a planting site, you need to distinguish between the main primary cultivated types of lavender. While all share an aromatic character and a love for gritty soil, their hardiness, bloom windows, and fragrance profiles differ. Decide whether you need cold-hardy sweetness, early theatrical blooms, or sweeping garden drama. Matching the type to your USDA zone and regional climate is your first step toward lasting vigor.

    Giving lavender the right start is key to years of aromatic, low-maintenance beauty. The ideal planting window depends on your local climate. In cold-winter regions (zones 5-7), set plants in the ground in mid-to-late spring, once all threat of frost has passed. This gives their relatively fragile roots a full growing season to establish before winter freezes arrive. Conversely, in warm southern and western areas (zones 8-10), you need to plant in fall to take advantage of cooling air temperatures while the soil remains warm, letting roots settle without heat stress.

    Whatever your zone, give your lavender plenty of elbow room. Crowding traps stagnant humidity around the foliage, encouraging fungal leaf blight. Space standard English varieties and compact hedges 2-3 feet (60-90cm) apart. Give larger hybrid lavandins a generous 3 to 4 feet (90-120cm) of breathing room. If in doubt, grab a Stanley Fatmax Tape Measure from The Home Depot to ensure you give your plants enough room to maintain their crisp notes and elegant shapes.

    In a recent development, when lifting young specimens from nursery pots, resist the urge to vigorously tease apart the root ball. Lavender has a sensitive root network and resents rough handling. Loosen the outer circling root tips gently before settling the plant into place.

    To understand what lavender craves, picture a craggy Mediterranean hillside: crumbly, sun-baked, and full of stones. Heavy, water-retentive clay is lavender’s nemesis. If your native soil feels sticky or drains poorly after rain, avoid adding fine builder’s sand, which binds with clay particles to form an impenetrable barrier. Instead, work in generous amounts of coarse horticultural grit, pumice, perlite or crushed gravel. You can buy pouches of Plantonix Organic Perlite from Amazon.

    In a recent development, also, if your soil leans on the acidic side (typical in piney or damp eastern backyards), dust the planting area with some garden lime to lift the soil pH and make it more alkaline. While Spanish lavender is slightly more forgiving of neutral soils, English varieties won’t compromise. When in doubt, build a gentle mound or raised mound bed. Elevating roots even 6 inches (15cm) can make a world of difference.

    Lavender is a lusty sun-lover that doesn’t want to compromise on light. To maintain high concentrations of aromatic essential oils, these plants need a minimum of 6 hours of direct, unfiltered sunlight daily, with 8 or more hours preferred. Planting in partial shade can lead to leggy growth, sparse flowering, and floppy support.

    Sources indicate that position your lavender along a south or west-facing brick wall, a flanking stone path, or nestled beside a gravel terrace. These surfaces help to absorb warmth during peak daylight hours and then re-emit heat in the evening. Just as importantly, the presence of stone and gravel can accelerate the evaporation of dew and rain, keeping foliage dry and reducing the incidence of fungal leaf spot.

    Taking a methodical approach at planting time helps your young lavender transition happily from nursery pot to garden dwelling. You need to set the correct root depth, establish good drainage, and avoid burying the woody crown. Do all this, and you can eliminate the risk of shock. Follow these steps to set your lavender up for vigorous, drought-resistant growth:.

    Lavender is the ultimate low-maintenance perennial, provided you don't smother it with affection. If your usual gardening instinct involves wandering around with a watering can and tucking plants into cozy damp bark, you can relax. Lavender doesn’t want royal treatment. Think of ongoing care as gentle stewardship based on its Mediterranean temperament. Give it baking sun, dry roots, and an occasional appreciative nod, and it will reward you with months of fragrant abundance.

    During their first 6-8 weeks in the ground, young plants require consistent hydration. Provide a deep soaking once a week when the top 2 inches (5cm) of soil dry out. Once established, lavender is fiercely drought-tolerant. Mature English cultivars (L. angustifolia) and vigorous hybrid lavandins (L. × intermedia) thrive for weeks on natural rainfall alone and need supplemental water only during extended droughts. Spanish varieties might need an occasional sip when the dog days hit, but that’s it.

    Sources indicate that always apply water directly to the base using a narrow-spout watering can. Something like the Yowon Long Spout Gold Watering Can from Amazon can help you deliver water straight to the root zone. Avoid overhead watering, which can trigger leaf spot. Of course, terracotta container-grown specimens dry out faster than bed-planted shrubs, so just check weekly during peak summer heat.

    Lavender is naturally adapted to lean soils formed over weathered limestone, so its nutritional requirements are low. In fact, over-fertilizing is one of the quickest ways to ruin an established plant. Heavy applications of nitrogen-rich feeds trigger sappy growth at the expense of floral buds, and can also reduce the concentration of fragrant linalool and camphor oils that give lavender its signature aroma.

    Instead of routine feeding, rely on soil conditioning. If your soil is nutrient-depleted, top-dress in early spring with an ultra-thin layer of well-aged organic compost or a light scattering of bone meal and greensand. You can buy Down to Earth Bone Meal from Walmart for a slow-release treat. In containers, a half-strength seaweed feed is also fine once a season. While French hybrid lavandins can handle a whisper of nutrition in spring, though, classic English varieties prefer to stay lean.

    Spreading shredded hardwood, bark nuggets, or damp leaf mold around the base of lavender is a mistake. Organic wood mulches retain excessive moisture, slow evaporation, and harbor fungal spores. Furthermore, dark, damp bark cools the soil surface. The secret to proper lavender mulching lies in crunchy mineral alternatives. Crushed limestone is a favorite for English varieties, as it slowly releases calcium into the soil. Spanish cultivars love granite grit for keeping crowns high and dry.

    Add a crisp, two-inch (5cm) layer of light-colored pea gravel, crushed limestone, or even crushed oyster seashells across the planting bed. Gravel does not rot and lets rainwater drain promptly. Pale stones act like sun reflectors, bouncing daylight right up into the underbelly of the plant. You can buy Rain Forest White Pea Gravel from The Home Depot for a reflective base that reflects sunlight back up into the foliage.

    Industry observers note that transplanting established lavender is challenging. This is because lavender forms a deep, brittle root network that resents disturbance. Older, woody plants rarely survive being moved, as severed roots struggle to regenerate in heavy soils. If relocation is essential, attempt only in early spring, just as fresh growth begins to show. Never transplant in midsummer or the damp cold of late fall.

    To transplant lavender, prepare the newly introduced planting hole with coarse grit and lime. Dig wide and deep around the lavender to carry as much of the root along as you can. Once settled into its new home, give the top branches a trim, cutting back the soft green growth by about a third. This takes the pressure off the roots while they settle in and helps to reduce the risk of moisture stress.

    According to recent reports, pruning is notable if you want to keep your lavender in good shape. Doing this at least once a year helps to prevent splayed dead centers, and encourages flower production (and better fragrance!). However, there is one non-negotiable: never cut back into the old bare wood. Unlike deciduous shrubs, mature lavender wood is not likely to regenerate. Shearing into the gnarled brown center often results in permanent branch dieback or the loss of the entire shrub.

    Recent findings suggest that there are two seasonal stages. In early spring, once the first leaf shoots emerge from the lower stems, conduct a light wake-up trim. Snip away frost-damaged tips and gently shape the edges, taking care not to prune too early while hard freezes still threaten. Then in summer, after the main flowering ends, it’s time for the main structural cut. Using sharp bypass shears, clip away all spent flowers and remove one-third of the current season's soft green growth to form a smooth, rounded dome. This dome will help to shed any winter snow and also encourages dense branching.

    Sources indicate that tailor your approach to your variety’s personality. Substantial French lavandins can take a confident, thorough haircut to tame wild wands, while compact English types prefer a gentle, elegant shaping. If you’re growing Spanish lavender with its rabbit-ear blooms, simply snip spent flower heads through spring to keep blooms coming. If you need a good snipping tool, you can buy Spear & Jackson CuttingSet8 Traditional Bypass & Anvil Secateur Set from Amazon. Just tuck the shears away before fall chills roll in.

    Grow the right cultivar in the right place, and you can enjoy decades-long beauty. Breeders have refined lavender to excel in specific roles, from compact edging to storm-resistant mounds. These 5 standouts deliver exceptional performance, pest resistance, and exquisite blooms:.

    There’s no getting around the fact that lavender success will depend on where you live. In the high heat and summer humidity of the Southeastern US and Gulf Coast, fungal melt is the biggest glitch. Overcome this by planting in raised beds, doubling planting distances to 4 feet (1.2m) for better airflow, and choosing humidity-tolerant French hybrids (like Phenomenal or Sensational) rather than traditional English types.

    According to recent reports, in severe northern zones (zones 4-5), deep winter freezes and dry winds can cause severe dieback. In these areas, stick to true English cultivars (Munstead or Hidcote), which tolerate sub-zero temperatures. Keep shrubs in well-drained soil on sheltered slopes where snow can form a natural blanket. And avoid late-season fertilization as this delays dormancy.

    In the sun-drenched, alkaline West and Southwest (zones 8-10), native conditions closely mirror the Mediterranean. Spanish lavenders and French toothed types thrive in lean native soils. The primary danger here is over-irrigation from lawn sprinklers. So just be sensible about your watering.

    Growing lavender in pots is a dream, as long as you are thoughtful about drainage and watering. Containers are certainly an excellent workaround if you have heavy clay or damp native soil. However, stick to thick-walled, unglazed terracotta or breathable stone composite. Unglazed clay is naturally porous, allowing excess moisture to evaporate through the walls and ensuring critical root respiration.

    Make sure your pot has a generous drainage hole. It’s also a good idea to elevate pots onto pot feet or risers to prevent drainage outlets sealing flat against patio stones. You can get Doggy Plant Pot Feet from Amazon to elevate heavy planters an inch off patio surfaces, guaranteeing free drainage flow and preventing trapped moisture.

    For the potting blend, you need a super-gritty cocktail. Mix seven parts light potting compost with three parts chunky perlite or volcanic pumice. Never use potting mixes containing synthetic gel crystals. While bed-grown lavender rarely needs water once established, container roots dry rapidly. Water deeply only when the top 2 inches (5cm) is bone dry. Rotate each pot in your lavender container garden a quarter-turn every week, so plants receive balanced light for the liveliest, bee-friendly results.

    Recent findings suggest that the best winter survival for lavender isn’t about fighting freezing temperatures, but preventing excess slush. This hinges on shielding lavender from standing wet and gales. In beds, cold-hardy English varieties and vigorous lavandins tolerate sub-zero temperatures down to zone 5. Just keep the root crown clear of soggy leaf debris, and erect a burlap windbreak in exposed northern sites.

    In a recent development, potted specimens are more vulnerable. In zone 6 and colder, move containers into an unheated garage, shed, or sheltered cold frame once nighttime temperatures consistently drop below 30°F (-1°C). Give them just a small cup of water once a month. Use Bloem Plant Caddies from The Home Depot to help wheel heavier containers inside.

    Sources indicate that if you're growing Spanish varieties, bring them indoors to a bright, cool windowsill before hard freezes arrive. Once the spring sun warms the patio and frost warnings disappear, ease pots back outdoors, hardening them off gradually in dappled shade.

    Recent findings suggest that propagating lavender from stem cuttings is far more reliable than starting from seed, and the results of growing from lavender cuttings can be enormously satisfying. Lavender seed can be erratic, with low germination rates, and hybrid lavandins produce sterile seed that will not come true to type. Taking cuttings ensures a clone that preserves your parent’s exact flower color, growth habit and essential oil profile. You just need to be selective about timing and plant age.

    According to recent reports, the best time for taking lavender cuttings is mid-summer to early fall, using semi-ripe wood. These are stems of the current season’s growth that are firm and woody at the base but still green at the tip. Select healthy non-flowering shoots from vigorous, 2-4-year-old plants. Strip the foliage from the lower 2 inches (5cm) of a 3-4-inch stem, gently scraping a sliver of outer bark at the base. Dip the cut tip in rooting hormone and insert it into a sharp 50/50 mix of coarse horticultural sand and perlite.

    Optionally, you can pop a clear plastic bag over the pot like a mini greenhouse. Then maintain bright, indirect light and gentle bottom warmth, keeping the rooting medium just barely damp. Roots normally develop in 4-6 weeks, which you can tell if you feel a resistance when you gently tug the cutting. Overwinter the young starts in a frost-free frame, planting them out into sunny borders in spring.

    One of the best things about lavender’s scent is that it is a natural deterrent for most garden pests and troublemakers, including deer and rabbits. When lavender does encounter problems, it usually stems from environmental imbalances like stagnant airflow and heavy soils. Here are some of the main challenges your plant might face:.

    Industry observers note that lavender is naturally woody and develops hard, bare interior branches as it ages. This usually happens due to skipped annual pruning or improper shearing. Over time, outer branches get heavy, exposing the leafless core. While you cannot cut back into bare old wood to rejuvenate it, you can prevent it getting more pronounced. Prune annually in late summer by removing one-third of the soft green growth.

    Unlike herbaceous perennials such as hostas or coneflowers, lavender is a true woody bush. All fresh growth must regenerate from active leaf nodes along the soft upper stems. If you cut beneath the lowest leafy nodes into the bare brown wood, the branch cannot recover. Always leave at least 2-3 inches (5-8cm) of green foliage intact when you’re trimming back.

    Recent findings suggest that harvest on a warm, dry morning, once dew has evaporated. Ideally, cut stems when the bottom third of the florets have opened, but before the upper buds burst. At this stage, the concentration of essential oils is at its peak. Secure the cut stems in loose bundles with bands or twine for good air movement. Hang upside down in a dark, dry, airy space for 2-3 weeks. Keeping them out of direct sunlight locks in color.

    Standard English varieties struggle with intense southern humidity and wet soils. High atmospheric moisture traps dampness against foliage, inviting fungal rot. If you garden in the south, plant in sharply draining raised beds or rock gardens amended with coarse grit. Better yet, choose humidity-tolerant French hybrids like Phenomenal or Sensational, bred to hold its own in sweltering southern summer heat.

    Life is sweeter with a little lavender in it. Whether you want to carve out a sun-baked border for a cloud of bumbles, frame your walkway with a billowing fragrant hedge, or cultivate a terracotta pot of blooms on a balcony, lavender elevates every space as surely as it plays with the senses. So come on, expand your purple horizons, and get ready to fall head over heels with a lifelong cottage garden icon….

    Move Over, Potpourri – These 6 Fragrant Plants Fill a Room With Natural Christmas Scent

    • Recent findings suggest that nothing creates a cozy Christmas atmosphere quite like a home filled with beautiful seasonal aromas – but instead of reaching for scented candles, air fresheners or potpourri, why not let living plants provide a naturally wonderful fragrance?
    • Sources indicate that while Christmas cactus, amaryllis and poinsettia top the lists of holiday houseplants for their fabulous flowers, there are plenty of plants that deserve a spot in your home for their fragrance, too.
    • Think beyond the usual seasonal smells of pine or warming spices and use these seasonal houseplants to enjoy sweet, fresh, floral, woodsy and even chocolatey aromas to scent your home this year.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that nothing creates a cozy Christmas atmosphere quite like a home filled with beautiful seasonal aromas – but instead of reaching for scented candles, air fresheners or potpourri, why not let living plants provide a naturally wonderful fragrance? The holidays are rich with aromas from pine-scented garlands to pumpkin pies baking in the oven, and using Christmas plants to bring another layer of perfume makes your home feel even more warm and inviting.

    Sources indicate that while Christmas cactus, amaryllis and poinsettia top the lists of holiday houseplants for their fabulous flowers, there are plenty of plants that deserve a spot in your home for their fragrance, too. Alongside attractive greenery and beautiful blooms, these scented selections will add to the festive ambience.

    Think beyond the usual seasonal smells of pine or warming spices and use these seasonal houseplants to enjoy sweet, fresh, floral, woodsy and even chocolatey aromas to scent your home this year.

    According to recent reports, for a traditional Christmas fragrance with unique notes, rosemary (Salvia rosmarinus) should be a staple for the holidays. This woody perennial herb is evergreen and has a piney aroma mixed with citrus, floral and mint notes that works so well with more traditional holiday scents. You could trim your potted rosemary like a topiary into a Christmas tree profile, or leave it in its natural bushy shape and pluck stems to tuck among roast potatoes or plunge into holiday cocktails.

    While traditional rosemary is fabulous just as it is, other varieties can offer more in the way of holiday decor and still be used in the kitchen. Tuscan Blue rosemary, available from trees.com, has the same pleasing scent with particularly glossy leaves (and highly ornamental blue blooms in spring and summer). Arp rosemary, available from Burpee, has the strongest fragrance of all and while it's capable of growing into a big plant outside, it's easy to keep small in a pot.

    Industry observers note that provide a potted rosemary with bright light, ideally from a south-facing window, and potting soil that drains very well. Rosemary naturally grows in warm, dry climates but indoors it prefers cooler temperatures and a little more moisture, so just let the top inch of soil dry between waterings. This is a tough, adaptable plant so it can be grown outside year-round in zones 8-10, or simply pop it outdoors for spring and summer in colder zones.

    Recent findings suggest that forcing bulbs indoors is a fun holiday project and paperwhites (Narcissus papyraceus) are among the easiest to grow. The delicate white blooms resemble daffodils and grow elegantly on tall stems, with a floral fragrance that complements other seasonal scents well. Grown in a decorative dish or bowl, paperwhites offer sophisticated décor and delicious perfume in one.

    Unlike other bulbs, narcissus don’t require a chill period so there's still time to get holiday blooms if you hurry, as it only takes three to six weeks to force paperwhite bulbs. A good bet are Ziva paperwhite bulbs, available from Eden Brothers, as they're effortlessly elegant and the easiest to grow. For a little more frill, Erlicheer paperwhite bulbs, also available from Eden Brothers, enjoy the same appealing fragrance and even more petals.

    In a recent development, use shallow containers with potting mix or glass dishes with decorative gravel, which allows you to see the bulbs and some of the roots as they grow. In zones 9-11, paperwhites can be replanted outdoors once they've finished flowering.

    Industry observers note that for a floral perfume that carries the promise of spring, forced hyacinth bulbs are a must for the holidays. Hyacinths (Hyacinthus orientalis) smell intensely floral with notes of green growth, sweet honey and wholesome earthiness. As with paperwhites, you can grow these bulbs in containers with soil or use decorative glass containers to show off their interesting roots.

    Industry observers note that bulbs need to be chilled for 10 to 14 weeks, then blooms takes three to four weeks to grow, so you'll need to buy pre-planted holiday hyacinths for flowers this year, which you'll find at some grocery stores as well as garden centers. But pop a note into your phone calendar now to remind yourself to plant hyacinth bulbs in September for bowls of fragrant Christmas flowers.

    In a recent development, once they bloom, keep your hyacinths in a cool spot to preserve the flowers for as long as possible. After flowering, you can replant bulbs outside in zones 4-8.

    It has been revealed that cupressus macrocarpa ‘Goldcrest’ is a variety of lemon cypress in a unique shade of yellow-green with a delicious citrus aroma. If you feel that holiday scents are sometimes a little too sweet and cloying, this is the plant you need to balance that with a fresh, clean perfume. As this evergreen is Christmas tree-shaped, lemon cypress adds a upcoming element to traditional holiday greenery too.

    A great option for growing in a pot is the dwarf lemon cypress 'Wilma Goldcrest', available from trees.com. Though capable of eventually growing to 6 feet high and 1-2 feet wide, by growing this compact form in a planter, you can easily keep it small enough to bring indoors as a holiday houseplant for many years to come.

    Position lemon cypress where the foliage will be brushed against as this is how the aroma is released, or you can simply crush the foliage between finger and thumb for a fresh burst of fragrance whenever you fancy. Your lemon cypress will need bright light but fairly cool temperatures. Water the pot regularly to avoid total dryness, but don’t let the roots sit in soggy soil. This compact tree grows best outdoors so move it outside after the holidays in zones 7-11, or overwinter indoors as a houseplant in zones 3-6.

    Scented geraniums (Pelargonium spp.) offer the ultimate opportunity to customize your holiday fragrance profile. There are varieties with foliage that smells like roses, citrus, apple, ginger, cinnamon, chocolate mint and even nutmeg. Mix and match or pair with other houseplants to concoct a signature Christmas scent.

    At this time of the year, the best place to find plants is via the Etsy scented geranium live plants hub which lists available stock from verified independent nurseries. You’ll get the most out of your scented geraniums by placing them where you can rub the leaves to release a burst of fragrance. They need a sunny spot, too, as well as soil that drains well. Water when the soil begins to dry and pinch back stems to keep the foliage dense.

    Scented geraniums can be grown outdoors year-round in zones 10-11, while in cooler climates they're best treated as winter houseplants that enjoy the summer outside on a sunny patio.

    According to recent reports, for a unique chocolatey aroma, Oncidium Heaven Scent 'Redolence' is an orchid with a wonderfully sweet chocolate fragrance. You’ll also enjoy the elegant spikes of burgundy and white flowers that last for a month or more. Look out, too, for Oncidium Aka Baby 'Raspberry Chocolate' with a lighter but no less lovely chocolate perfume.

    It's best to buy speciality orchids from specialist nurseries, and to be sure you’ll have aromatic flowers for the holidays, buy a plant that is already in bud or bloom. Akatsuka Orchid Gardens is one such nursery, based in Hawaii and stocking both the Heaven Scent 'Redolence' orchid and 'Raspberry Chocolate' orchid in bud and bloom. These orchids grow best in bright but indirect light and in a potting mix designed specifically for orchids. Water when the mix is dry and avoid overwatering or letting the mix get soggy. Good air circulation is also a must, and keep orchids as houseplants year-round.

    A few simple practices will keep your aromatic holiday houseplants fresh and fragrant:.

    Mary Ellen Ellis has been gardening for over 20 years. With degrees in Chemistry and Biology, Mary Ellen's specialties are flowers, native plants, and herbs.

    #21457. No Need to Throw Out That Old Potting Soil – These 6 Unfussy Plants Will Happily Grow in It

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1118 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Gardeningknowhow ↗ Open Full Page

    No Need to Throw Out That Old Potting Soil – These 6 Unfussy Plants Will Happily Grow in It

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1118 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Once you’ve cleaned out your summer containers, you might think it’s best to tip the remaining potting mix into the waste.
    • Sources indicate that over the growing season, that potting soil loses some nutrients because plants take them up and water washes them away.
    • Some plants actually prefer leaner soil.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Once you’ve cleaned out your summer containers, you might think it’s best to tip the remaining potting mix into the waste. Don’t be too hasty. That mix could still have plenty of life left in it.

    Sources indicate that over the growing season, that potting soil loses some nutrients because plants take them up and water washes them away. Bulky materials, like peat moss and compost, break down over the summer, too. However, reusing potting soil is possible as long as the previous residents didn’t have diseases or serious pest infestations.

    Some plants actually prefer leaner soil. Here, I describe six plants that are capable of thriving in old potting mix. I also provide some tips for refreshing the soil to give the upcoming plants a little boost.

    Nasturtium (Tropaeolum majus) is a beautiful flowering plant that grows as an annual in most gardens. Many types trail or vine, making them ideal for containers. The brilliant flowers come in shades of red, yellow, and orange, like in these Jewel Blend nasturtium seeds from Seed Needs on Amazon, which also offers other beautiful color mixes. Both the flowers and leaves are edible. If you live in USDA zone 9 or warmer, you can grow nasturtiums as perennials.

    Sources indicate that nasturtiums are good candidates for recycled potting mix because they are unfussy, easy to grow, and generally thrive in poor soil. They are also easy to grow from seed. Sow seeds in your used potting mix next year when it’s warm enough. Place the container in a sunny spot and water when the top inch of soil dries.

    Moss rose (Portulaca grandiflora) is another annual in most gardens. This low-growing succulent, native to South America, blooms in summer and fall with flowers that resemble small roses. You can find a lovely selection of moss rose seed varieties at Eden Brothers, with a choice of colors to brighten up your containers. Moss rose thrives in poor, rocky, or sandy soil, making it ideal for containers. Plants need good drainage, so they can sometimes struggle in beds with heavy soil or poor drainage.

    Sources indicate that grow your moss roses in reused potting mix enhanced with perlite, like this Riare organic perlite on Amazon, or something similar to boost drainage. Place them in a full-sun spot and let the soil dry out in between waterings. Avoid overfertilizing, which can lead to more leaves and fewer flowers.

    Industry observers note that sedums (Sedum spp.) are reliable and popular perennials for garden beds, but they also grow well in containers. This is a large group of plants, many of which are succulents suited to dry, poor soil. Many gardeners love stonecrops like ‘Autumn Joy,’ which turn gorgeous shades of deep red in fall. You can buy Autumn Joy sedum from Nature Hills to enjoy its colorful late-season display. You can also choose from among low-growing and taller clump-forming sedums.

    The most important part of refreshing old soil for growing sedum is to add a material, like perlite, to improve drainage. Place your pots in a sunny location and water only when the soil dries. Avoid using too much, if any, fertilizer.

    In a recent development, hens and chicks (Sempervivum spp.) are diminutive succulents that grow in rosettes and have delightfully fleshy leaves that can be bluish-green, copper, gold, reddish, or even two-toned. You can enjoy a mix of varieties with this hens and chicks plant collection from Hirt's Gardens Store on Amazon. While hens and chicks flower, they are grown mostly for their attractive foliage. Hardy perennials in many growing regions, hens and chicks also make great container plants. They produce small offsets, the chicks, that can be repotted for propagation.

    Hens and chicks naturally grow in poor, rocky soil, so they should do well in your spent potting mix. Just be sure to add additional material to boost drainage. The best containers for hens and chicks are shallow and have adequate drainage holes, like this Deroma clay bowl planter from Target. Grow them in full sun or very light shade and water sparingly, letting the potting mix dry between waterings.

    Calendula (Calendula officinalis), also known as pot marigold, is a short-lived perennial in zones 9 through 11, and an annual elsewhere. Though it is considered a flowering herb, many people grow calendula solely for its ornamental value. The flowers are daisy-like and usually bright orange or yellow, although they can also be red, white, or pink. You can pick up calendula seeds cheaply on Amazon, but Eden Brothers offers some gorgeous varieties, including the Pacific Beauty Mix and the Sunset Buff calendula pictured here.

    Recent findings suggest that A Mediterranean native, calendula appreciates warmth, sunlight, and well-draining soil. It won’t tolerate soggy soil. It can thrive in poor soil but benefits from a little refresh of old potting mix with compost. Water your potted calendula regularly, but don’t let the soil get waterlogged. Deadhead the flowers throughout the season to encourage additional blooms.

    Like calendula, cosmos (Cosmos bipinnatus) are mostly grown as annuals and are only hardy in zones 9 and higher. Cosmos are easy to grow from seed and reward you with feathery foliage and delicate flowers in shades of red, pink, white, yellow, and orange. Burpee sells a wide variety of cosmos seeds, including the beautiful ‘Sensation Mix’ pictured here. They make great cut flowers.

    While cosmos tolerate poor soil, it’s best to refresh the old potting mix a little. Then, you can sow seeds and place the pot in a location with full sun. Use a large container, as cosmos can grow quite tall. Water the seeds and seedlings regularly to keep the soil moist, and then only sparingly.

    Industry observers note that while all of these, and many other plants, tolerate leaner soil, all plants will appreciate a little refresh of old, tired soil. A few simple steps will give you better results over the course of the growing season:.

    Remember that not all old soil should be used. Disease and pests can be passed on, so don’t take the risk. Also, if you’re growing plants that aren’t as tough as those listed here, it’s best to start over with fresh potting mix. You should also replace the mix if it has broken down so much that it becomes muddy and dense when wet.

    Remember, old potting soil doesn’t necessarily belong in the trash. With a little refreshing and by choosing the right plants, you can recycle that old mix and use it for at least one more year.

    Mary Ellen Ellis has been gardening for over 20 years. With degrees in Chemistry and Biology, Mary Ellen's specialties are flowers, native plants, and herbs.

    #21455. Sarah Jessica Parker's Christmas Tree Trick Is Stunning – And All You Need Is Baby's Breath

    📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (862 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Gardeningknowhow ↗ Open Full Page

    Sarah Jessica Parker's Christmas Tree Trick Is Stunning – And All You Need Is Baby's Breath

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (862 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Thanks to her stint in The Family Stone, Sarah Jessica Parker's name has long been synonymous with the holidays for fans – and even more so now she's shared her Christmas tree trick with us all!
    • Yes, it is now possible to give your Christmas tree that Carrie Bradshaw stamp of approval!
    • This underrated flower has spent most of its life being a supporting actor to bigger and better roses, or a wispy filler flower tucked into grocery store bouquets.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Thanks to her stint in The Family Stone, Sarah Jessica Parker's name has long been synonymous with the holidays for fans – and even more so now she's shared her Christmas tree trick with us all!

    Yes, it is now possible to give your Christmas tree that Carrie Bradshaw stamp of approval! And, somewhat gloriously, SJP's approach to festive decor has the same sort of wonderfully unfussy vibe as Michelle Obama's twig tree, which means you don't need a celebrity-sized budget to recreate the look. In fact, all you really need is baby's breath.

    This underrated flower has spent most of its life being a supporting actor to bigger and better roses, or a wispy filler flower tucked into grocery store bouquets. But when Kristin Davis posted an Instagram video of herself arranging flowers blindfolded (as one does), Sarah Jessica Parker left a surprising comment: “You can use babies breath in your Christmas tree.” Say what?

    Now, Kristin Davis (who worked at a florist in college) wasn’t keen on using it for her own tree (very Charlotte-coded), but she did share a rule worth stealing: if you're going to do it, then always arrange flowers in odd numbers, like three or five.

    According to recent reports, for me, though, SJP’s comment about using baby’s breath in her Christmas tree has set my imagination alight! And with that in mind, I asked some experts how I could use them in my own holiday decoration this year.

    The biggest risk when it comes to stealing Sarah Jessica Parker's idea is overdoing it. Roberta Sabbatini, founder of ItalianTouch Events, notes, “The main mistake is using too much. The beauty of baby’s breath is its lightness.” Morgan Brooks of Plant Style Home puts it even better, saying, “One loose spiral is elegant. Three is a snowstorm, and the tree disappears behind it.”.

    Remember that odd-number rule? CEO of Florals Memories Nadi Melam clips her baby’s breath into “clouds” and adds them in threes, noting, “Baby’s breath looks beautiful on trees because of negative space.” Translation: let the tree breathe!

    According to recent reports, for a spiral, Brooks gathers five to seven stems, wires each bunch at the base, and tucks the ends deep into the branches. Sabbatini also skips pushing loose stems into the tree and instead secures each little bundle with florist wire or ribbon.

    Fresh baby’s breath is a diva out of water. Brooks states fresh stems “wilt within a day or two indoors,” while dried versions keep their shape all season and can be packed away for next year. Melam agrees that dried is “far easier to work with.” If you do love fresh, just be sure to add it on Christmas Eve.

    If you don't have time for the drying process, this Bexikou dried baby’s breath bouquet comes ready to use, and its short white stems are well suited to wiring into small, airy clusters for your tree.

    Drying your own for a Sarah Jessica Parker-style tree is simple. Bundle five to seven stems with twine, hang them upside down in a dark, warm, well-ventilated room, and check after five days, as outlined in our guide to growing baby’s breath. If you’re short on time, ready-dried bunches work just as well.

    On an artificial tree, Brooks adds fine floral wire around the branch wire, since the stems are too light to stay put when someone brushes past.

    Warm white lights, clear glass ornaments, and velvet ribbon are baby’s breath’s best friends. Brooks adds pearl baubles and silver or soft gold ribbon to the list, but warns that rustic burlap and heavy red ornaments “fight it.” Treat baby’s breath as one of just two or three ideas on the tree, not the whole script.

    Pair your baby’s breath with a strand of Northlight 100-count warm white LED mini lights, which stay cool to the touch and give the soft, candlelit glow that suits a delicate white filler.

    Recent findings suggest that dried stems are brittle and, as Melam notes, highly flammable. Use cool LED lights and keep bunches away from hot bulbs and open flames. Baby’s breath is also mildly toxic to cats, so if pets are around, keep it to the upper two-thirds of the tree and sweep up anything that falls.

    Recent findings suggest that baby’s breath is easy to grow, so sow seeds next spring, cut and dry the blooms in summer, and next December’s tree is sorted. Will your tree look like a Manhattan brownstone from a certain Sarah Jessica Parker-fronted TV series? Possibly, but only if you resist the urge to add a fourth bunch.
